'''Steven L. Peck''' (born July 25, 1957) is an American [[evolutionary biologist]], poet, and novelist. His literary work is influential in [[Mormon literature]] circles. He is a professor of [[biology]] at [[Brigham Young University]] (BYU). He grew up in [[Moab, Utah]], and lives in [[Pleasant Grove, Utah]].

After studying at BYU and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Peck received his PhD from North Carolina State University in biomathematics and entomology. He has taught bioethics and [[philosophy of biology]] in addition to other biology classes, and teaches that evolution is not at odds with religious faith.

Peck's fiction often defies genre conventions and discusses philosophical themes. Critics have praised his unusual stories for their emotional power and their analytical approach to Mormon themes. Both ''The Scholar of Moab'' and ''Gilda Trillum'' received the [[Association for Mormon Letters]] (AML) award for best novel, and Peck received the Smith-Petit Lifetime award from the AML in 2021.

==Education and career==
As a child, Peck enjoyed playing with toy dinosaurs and being outdoors. His father was a social worker who ran a camp in the [[Rocky Mountains]].<ref name=MICon/>

After failing high school history, Peck studied to receive his GED.<ref name="Organon">{{cite web|last1=Peck|first1=Steve|title=A BYU Bio-Professor Explores Science and Faith|url=http://sciencebysteve.net/about/|website=The Mormon Organon|access-date=12 January 2017|date=12 April 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161028153333/http://sciencebysteve.net/about/|archive-date=28 October 2016}}</ref>

He joined the Army after the Vietnam War, and was reactivated in [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] (LDS Church) shortly afterwards. He served an LDS mission in Arkansas.<ref name=MICon>{{cite AV media
 | people =
 | title = Steven Peck and Terryl Givens, "The God Who Marvels" (Maxwell Institute Conversations)
 | medium = podcast
 | publisher = BYU Maxwell Institute
 | location =
 | date = June 29, 2018
 | url = https://mi.byu.edu/mic-peck/}}</ref>

Peck received a bachelor's degree in 1986 from BYU in [[statistics]] and [[computer science]], with a minor in [[zoology]]. He received a master's degree from [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in environmental biostatistics, and his PhD from [[North Carolina State University]] in [[biomathematics]] and [[entomology]] in 1997.<ref name=Patten>{{cite web |last1=Patten |first1=Lynn |title=Evolution and Faith to be Discussed at BYU's Summerhays Lecture |url=https://news.byu.edu/news/evolution-and-faith-be-discussed-byus-summerhays-lecture |website=News |publisher=University Communications |language=en |date=15 September 2016}}</ref> His dissertation was titled "Spatial Patterns and Processes in the Evolution of Insecticide Resistance."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Peck |first1=Steven L. |title=Curriculum Vita |url=https://brightspotcdn.byu.edu/00/0e/37a2d98024bb9d182aa657525ab3/954809967-cv-attachment.pdf |access-date=19 January 2022}}</ref>

He started teaching in the biology department at BYU in 2000, where he teaches bioethics and the history and philosophy of biology, among other classes.<ref name=Patten/><ref name=Hodges/>

In his work on decreasing insect-borne illness, Peck has worked as a consultant on projects with the [[United Nations]] [[International Atomic Energy Agency]] and the U.S. Department of Agriculture.<ref name=Hodges>{{cite web |last1=Hodges |first1=Blair |title=Available for pre-order: Evolving Faith, by Steven L. Peck |url=https://mi.byu.edu/pre-order-evolving-faith-peck/ |website=Neal A. Maxwell Institute |publisher=BYU Maxwell Institute |access-date=20 January 2022 |date=26 August 2015}}</ref> He has also worked on a consultant project with the Korean Federation of Science and Technology.<ref name=Patten/>

==Works==
{{main|Steven L. Peck bibliography}}

Peck has published many scientific articles on ecology and ecological simulations in his work as a professor of biology at BYU. The topics of his literary works include evolution and religion.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mapping Literary Utah - Steven L. Peck |url=https://mappingliteraryutah.org/utah-writers/steven-l-peck |website=mappingliteraryutah.org |access-date=20 January 2022 |language=en-gb}}</ref>

[[Terryl Givens]] stated that Peck's work is "full of theological and metaphysical insight and probing".<ref name=MICon/>{{rp|38:09}} In a review for ''Dialogue'', [[Mormon fiction]] scholar Michael Austin wrote that Peck is "one of Mormonism's best living writers" and that he writes with "a genre-busting literary style."<ref name="Austin">{{cite journal|last1=Austin|first1=Michael|date=Spring 2016|title=Review: Peck's Peak. Wandering Realities: The Mormonish Short Fiction of Steven L. Peck. Evolving Faith: Wanderings of a Mormon Biologist|url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/articles/review-pecks-peak-steven-l-peck-wandering-realities-themormonish-short-fiction-of-steven-l-pecksteven-l-peck-evolving-faith-wanderings-of-a-mormon-biologist/|journal=Dialogue: A Journal of Mormon Thought|volume=49|issue=1}}</ref> In a book review of ''Wandering Realities'' published in ''BYU Studies'', Scott R. Parkin described Peck as possibly "the most important Mormon fiction writer producing today."<ref name=Parkin>{{cite journal |last1=Parkin |first1=Scott R. |title=Wandering Realities |journal=BYU Studies |date=2016 |volume=55 |issue=2 |url=https://byustudies.byu.edu/article/wandering-realities-the-mormonish-short-fiction-of-steven-l-peck/ |language=en}}</ref> He wrote that Peck's works are by people who identify with Mormonism to the extent that they no longer question their own identity as a Mormon, and react to conflict based on that identity.<ref name=Parkin/>

===Critical reception===
{{see also|The Scholar of Moab}}
In ''[[A Short Stay in Hell]]'' (2009), a man must find the book of his life's story among every possible book. David Spaltro described the novella as "one of the most original and powerfully moving things I’ve ever read", and has acquired the rights to adapt it into a film.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Desowitz|first1=Bill|title=A Short Stay in Hell Feature Planned|url=http://billdesowitz.com/a-short-stay-in-hell-feature-planned/|website=billdesowitz.com|access-date=12 January 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116144059/http://billdesowitz.com/a-short-stay-in-hell-feature-planned/|archive-date=16 January 2017}}</ref> Doug Gibson at the ''Standard Examiner'' wrote that a hell that contains an "eternity of the mundane" is a "pretty effective hell."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Gibson|first1=Doug|title='A Short Stay in Hell' is an odd, compelling novella about an eternity of the mundane|url=http://www.standard.net/Opinion/2014/01/24/A-Short-Stay-in-Hell-is-an-odd-compelling-novella-about-an-eternity-of-the-mundane|access-date=12 January 2017|work=Standard-Examiner|date=28 February 2014|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116203253/http://www.standard.net/Opinion/2014/01/24/A-Short-Stay-in-Hell-is-an-odd-compelling-novella-about-an-eternity-of-the-mundane|archive-date=16 January 2017}}</ref> Derek Lee at ''Rational Faiths'' wrote that the novella encouraged reflection on the nature of the afterlife and what living forever would mean.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Lee|first1=Derek|title=A Short Stay in Hell - A Book Review - Rational Faiths {{!}} Mormon Blog|url=http://rationalfaiths.com/a-short-stay-in-hell-a-book-review/|website=Rational Faiths|access-date=12 January 2017|date=23 March 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170113165905/http://rationalfaiths.com/a-short-stay-in-hell-a-book-review/|archive-date=13 January 2017}}</ref>

The short story collection ''Wandering Realities'' (2015) contains stories set on other worlds and this one, and many are "just plain weird" featuring "odd characters driven by peculiar demons, with each tale told in a different voice and structured in a unique way," as described by reviewer Scott R. Parkin in ''BYU Studies''.<ref name="Parkin" /> Parkin concluded that Peck's stories move Mormon storytelling beyond a critique of the church as an institution and towards and more analytical approach to the inner life of Mormon characters.<ref name="Parkin" /> Steve Evans said the stories were "wondrous and rich."<ref>{{cite web|last1=Evans|first1=Steve|date=27 July 2015|title=Review: Wandering Realities by Steven Peck|url=https://bycommonconsent.com/2015/07/26/review-wandering-realities-by-steven-peck/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303220655/https://bycommonconsent.com/2015/07/26/review-wandering-realities-by-steven-peck/|archive-date=3 March 2016|access-date=12 January 2017|website=By Common Consent, a Mormon Blog}}</ref>

In a summary of Peck's book ''Evolving Faith'' (2015), Michael Austin wrote, "Because all knowledge incorporates subjective assumptions, both religion and science require an element of faith." Literal interpretations of scripture cheat "both religion, by ignoring what the author of the text was really trying to tell us, and science, by setting up unnecessary oppositions between important religious principles and easily testable facts."<ref name="Austin" /> At the [[Association for Mormon Letters]] (AML), Heather Young wrote that ''Evolving Faith'' had "enlarged my appreciation for my time on earth and the part I can play in protecting its immeasurable gifts."<ref>{{cite web|last1=Young|first1=Heather|title=Peck, "Evolving Faith – Wanderings of a Mormon Biologist" (reviewed by Heather Young)|url=http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/reviews/older-reviews/peck-evolving-faith-wanderings-of-a-mormon-biologist-reviewed-by-heather-young/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116145514/http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/reviews/older-reviews/peck-evolving-faith-wanderings-of-a-mormon-biologist-reviewed-by-heather-young/|archive-date=16 January 2017|access-date=12 January 2017|website=associationmormonletters.org|publisher=Association for Mormon Letters}}</ref> At ''By Common Consent'', Steve Evans said that the book was "not for beginners" and uses terminology that is difficult to understand, and that the two parts of the book were not well-connected.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Evans|first1=Steve|date=19 October 2015|title=Book Review: Evolving Faith: Wanderings of a Mormon Biologist by Steven Peck|url=https://bycommonconsent.com/2015/10/18/book-review-evolving-faith-wanderings-of-a-mormon-biologist/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170113170619/https://bycommonconsent.com/2015/10/18/book-review-evolving-faith-wanderings-of-a-mormon-biologist/|archive-date=13 January 2017|access-date=12 January 2017|website=By Common Consent, a Mormon Blog}}</ref>

In conceiving the main character for ''Gilda Trillum'' (2017), Peck wrote vignettes for a fictional main character and her relationship with writing and the Association of Mormon Letters. Several readers believed her to be real. Peck has stated that he enjoys mixing fictional references with real ones in his fiction.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Reiss |first1=Jana |title=Another weird and wonderful Mormon novel from Steven Peck |url=https://religionnews.com/2017/09/15/another-weird-and-wonderful-mormon-novel-from-steven-peck/ |website=Religion News Service |access-date=20 January 2022 |date=15 September 2017}}</ref> Rachel Kirkwood, writing in ''Dialogue'', felt that the various narrative fragments did not achieve the "characterization and depth for which the book seems to reach", but acknowledged that "the insufficiency of the fragments has its own charm."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kirkwood |first1=Rachel |title=Review: A Philosophical Portrait in Pieces Steven L. Peck. Gilda Trillim: Shepherdess of Rats |website=www.dialoguejournal.com |date=2018 |volume=52 |issue=1 |url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/articles/review-a-philosophical-portrait-in-pieces-steven-l-peck-gilda-trillim-shepherdess-of-rats/}}</ref> In another ''Dialogue'' review, Shane R. Peterson wrote that the book's strength is in its meditations on Mormon theology, and that its weakness is its presentation through the frame story of another character's dissertation, which gives Gilda a "strange distance" from the reader.<ref name="Peterson">{{cite journal |last1=Peterson |first1=Shane R. |title=Review: On Apple Seeds, Rats, and the State of Mormon Literature |journal=Dialogue: A Journal of Mormon Thought |date=Winter 2017 |volume=50 |issue=4 |doi=10.5406/dialjmormthou.50.4.0143 |s2cid=246621286 |url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/articles/review-on-apple-seeds-rats-and-the-state-of-mormon-literature-steven-l-peck-gilda-trillim-shepherdess-of-rats/ |access-date=3 February 2022|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

''The Tragedy of King Leere, Goatherd of the La Sals'' (2019) received a starred review in ''Publishers Weekly'', where its setting was described as a "fascinating world of technological solutions to global warming".<ref>{{cite web |title=Sci-Fi/Fantasy/Horror Book Review: The Tragedy of King Leere, Goatherd of the La Sals by Steven L. Peck|url=https://www.publishersweekly.com/978-1-948218-01-6 |website=PublishersWeekly.com |access-date=19 January 2022 |language=en}}</ref> In ''Dialogue'', Kylie Nielson Turley noticed how the book is difficult to categorize, wondering if it is better to call it "a modern-day ecological interpretation of the famous Shakespearian familial tragedy" or "a dystopian novel that will haunt the reader with visions of a post-apocalyptic future". She concludes by praising the book as "a well-written and thought-provoking tragedy that can stand solidly on its own."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Turley |first1=Kylie Nielson |title=The Tragedy of King Leere, Goatherd of the La Sals |journal=Dialogue: A Journal of Mormon Thought |date=Fall 2019 |volume=52 |issue=3 |url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/themencode-pdf-viewer-sc/?tnc_pvfw=ZmlsZT1odHRwczovL3d3dy5kaWFsb2d1ZWpvdXJuYWwuY29tL3dwLWNvbnRlbnQvdXBsb2Fkcy9zYmkvYXJ0aWNsZXMvRGlhbG9ndWVfVjUyTjAzX3IzLnBkZiZzZXR0aW5ncz0xMTExMTEwMTExMTExMTExMTAwJmxhbmc9ZW4tVVM=#page=&zoom=&pagemode=}}</ref>{{rp|194; 198}}

===Awards and honors===
Peck's novels and short stories have received multiple awards. ''The Scholar of Moab'' won the award for best novel from the AML in 2011, and was a finalist for the Montaigne Medal in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|title=AML Awards 2011|url=http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/aml-awards/aml-awards-2011/|website=associationmormonletters.org|access-date=11 January 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170111131500/http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/aml-awards/aml-awards-2011/|archive-date=11 January 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Montaigne Medal Finalists|url=http://www.hofferaward.com/Montaigne-Medal-finalists.html#.WHae01UrKUl|website=www.hofferaward.com|access-date=11 January 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161209052733/http://www.hofferaward.com/Montaigne-Medal-finalists.html#.WHae01UrKUl|archive-date=9 December 2016}}</ref> "A Strange Report from the Church Archives" won second place in the [[Irreantum]] fiction contest in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|title=Irreantum|url=http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/aml-publications-documents/irreantum/|website=associationmormonletters.org|access-date=11 January 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170111091150/http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/aml-publications-documents/irreantum/|archive-date=11 January 2017}}</ref> Peck received the [[AML award]] for short fiction for "Two-Dog Dose" in 2014.<ref>{{cite web|title=AML Awards 2014|url=http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/aml-awards/aml-awards-2014/|website=associationmormonletters.org|access-date=11 January 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170111131606/http://associationmormonletters.org/blog/aml-awards/aml-awards-2014/|archive-date=11 January 2017}}</ref> His non-fiction essay, "Five Wagers on What Intelligent Life Elsewhere in the Universe Will Be Like", received second place from the 2015 analytical laboratory reader's awards.<ref>{{cite web|title=The 2015 Analytical Laboratory Readers' Awards - News {{!}} Analog Science Fiction|url=http://www.analogsf.com/about-analog/the-analytical-laboratory/|website=www.analogsf.com|access-date=12 January 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116143624/http://www.analogsf.com/about-analog/the-analytical-laboratory/|archive-date=16 January 2017}}</ref> ''Gilda Trillum'' received the 2017 AML award for best novel.<ref>{{cite web |title=2017 AML Awards |url=https://www.associationmormonletters.org/2018/03/2017-aml-awards/ |website=Dawning of a Brighter Day |access-date=19 January 2022 |date=24 March 2018}}</ref> In 2021, Peck received the AML Smith-Petit lifetime achievement award. The award citation praised his unusual fiction: "If Peck’s works are medicine, they are strong, strange, and sometimes bitter-tasting. But perhaps this dose is what we need. Peck’s unpredictability confronts both the casual and scholarly readers, both the faithful and faithless, forcing them to question stereotypes, simplistic binaries, and straightforward reversals."<ref>{{cite web |title=Steven L. Peck: The 2021 Smith-Pettit Foundation Award for Outstanding Contribution to Mormon Letters |url=https://www.associationmormonletters.org/2021/06/steven-l-peck-the-2021-smith-pettit-foundation-award-for-outstanding-contribution-to-mormon-letters/ |website=Dawning of a Brighter Day |publisher=Association for Mormon Letters |access-date=19 January 2022 |date=6 June 2021}}</ref>

==Views==
{{See also|Mormon views on evolution}}

Peck believes that God "only enters the universe through our consciousness."<ref name="Riess interview">{{cite news|last1=Riess|first1=Jana|title=Mormon views on evolution are evolving, says biologist|url=http://religionnews.com/2015/11/30/mormon-views-on-evolution-are-evolving-says-biologist/|access-date=12 January 2017|work=Religion News Service|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170402162056/http://religionnews.com/2015/11/30/mormon-views-on-evolution-are-evolving-says-biologist/|archive-date=2 April 2017}}</ref> He compares scriptural interpretation to scientific interpretation, in that both nature and scriptures are unchanging, but our understanding of them changes over the course of generations.<ref name="Riess interview"/>

On the subject of writing, Peck says that it is a way for him to explore the complexities in his life.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Tribune|first1=The Salt Lake|title=Utah books that (almost) slipped past us in 2015|url=http://www.sltrib.com/home/3325502-155/from-utah-outward-2015-books-with|access-date=12 January 2017|work=The Salt Lake Tribune|date=27 December 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170113172316/http://www.sltrib.com/home/3325502-155/from-utah-outward-2015-books-with|archive-date=13 January 2017}}</ref> He has stated that anything we do to build our knowledge of the universe helps to build the kingdom of God.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Jepson|first1=Eric W.|title=Steven L. Peck — Mormon Artist|url=http://mormonartist.net/interviews/steven-l-peck/|website=mormonartist.net|access-date=12 January 2017|date=November 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112152629/http://mormonartist.net/interviews/steven-l-peck/|archive-date=12 November 2016}}</ref>

As a missionary, Peck taught potential members that they had to renounce evolution before being baptized. As a student at BYU, he found that biology professors taught the theory of evolution in the same way it is taught in secular schools. Peck has since become an advocate for teaching that religion and evolution are not at odds.<ref name=wanders/> The LDS church currently has no official position on evolution, and Peck teaches evolution in his courses at BYU.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Stiles|first1=Emilie|title=BYU professor writes book examining evolution and faith – The Daily Universe|url=http://universe.byu.edu/2015/11/02/byu-professor-writes-book-examining-evolution-and-faith1/|access-date=17 January 2017|work=The Daily Universe|date=2 November 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118084150/http://universe.byu.edu/2015/11/02/byu-professor-writes-book-examining-evolution-and-faith1/|archive-date=18 January 2017}}</ref>

==Personal life==
During their honeymoon, Peck and his wife, Lori, were hit by a drunk driver in Oregon. They were badly injured, and recovered after six months.<ref name=MICon/><ref name="Organon"/> The experience led Peck to change his major from philosophy to statistics.<ref name=wanders>{{cite web |last1=Olsen |first1=Jessica |title=Biology professor wanders through madness, fiction, science |url=https://universe.byu.edu/2017/01/16/biology-professor-wanders-through-madness-fiction-science/ |website=The Daily Universe |date=16 January 2017}}</ref>

Peck and Lori have five children, and six grandchildren.<ref>{{cite web|title=Contributors|url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/sbi/articles/Dialogue_V43N01_224.pdf|publisher=Dialogue|access-date=12 January 2017|date=2010|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116143628/https://www.dialoguejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/sbi/articles/Dialogue_V43N01_224.pdf|archive-date=16 January 2017}}</ref>

In 2002, Peck experienced visual hallucinations and delusions caused by a bacterial brain infection.<ref name=madness/> The bacteria, ''[[Burkholderia pseudomallei]]'', entered his brain through his optic nerve during a research trip to Vietnam in 2001.<ref name=snap/> He wrote about the experience, and stated that it taught him about the nature of consciousness.<ref name=madness>{{cite journal |last1=Peck |first1=Steven |title=My Madness |journal=Dialogue: A Journal of Mormon Thought |date=2008 |url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/sbi/articles/Dialogue_V41N02_73.pdf|volume=21|issue=2}}</ref> On the podcast ''Snap Judgement'', Peck said that the experience taught him that Satan could block God's influence on him, which affected how he views religious belief.<ref name=snap>{{cite AV media
 | people = Ash Sanders, producer; Ryan Sweikert, lead producer and sound designer
 | title =Believable: A Short Stay in Hell
 | medium = podcast
 | publisher =Snap Judgement Studios
 | location =
 | date = 2020
 | access-date=14 February 2022
 | url =https://snapjudgment.org/story/a-short-stay-in-hell/ }}</ref> Peck lives in Pleasant Grove.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Peck |first1=Steven L. |title=StevenLPeck |url=https://twitter.com/stevenlpeck |work=Twitter |language=en}}</ref>
